frameworks.name: ICE Prioritization
frameworks.definition: Rank initiatives by Impact (how big a difference it makes), Confidence (how likely it is to work), and Ease (how hard it is to execute); highest-scoring items execute first.

frameworks.name: Value Acceleration Method
frameworks.definition: Acquisition.com scorecard that simultaneously maximizes business value and minimizes risk; flags key-man dependency and customer concentration as primary red flags.

frameworks.name: Cost-Plus vs. Value-Based Pricing
frameworks.definition: Two pricing models: cost-plus anchors price to input cost, limiting upside; value-based anchors price to buyer willingness-to-pay, which is uncapped and decoupled from vendor cost changes.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that businesses using cost-plus pricing (pricing based on input costs plus a margin) consistently make less money than businesses using value-based pricing (pricing based on buyer willingness-to-pay), because cost-plus caps upside at cost structure while value-based pricing is decoupled from costs and uncapped.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to any business with meaningful price elasticity headroom
claims.mechanism: Cost-plus pricing directly ties maximum price to input costs; value-based pricing anchors to buyer willingness-to-pay, which is independent of costs and can exceed cost-plus by multiples.
bounded_by: May not apply in regulated markets with government-mandated price ceilings
May not apply in pure commodity markets where buyers have full price transparency

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that for a business with extremely thin net margins (around 6%), a 6% price increase alone would roughly double net profit, because at low margins the incremental revenue from a price increase flows almost entirely to the bottom line.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: net margin approximately 6%
price increase does not cause proportional volume drop
claims.mechanism: When net margin is 6%, a 6% price increase on the same volume produces an additional 6% of revenue that has no corresponding cost increase, nearly doubling the 6% profit base.

numbers.axis: price increase magnitude relative to net margin base

bounded_by: Assumes volume does not drop proportionally; assumes fixed costs are already covered

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that not testing prices is the most expensive decision a business can make, because the profit left uncaptured from under-pricing exceeds the downside risk of testing a higher price (which can always be reversed).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: business with pricing that has never been systematically tested

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that in mature e-commerce businesses, 30 to 50% of total revenue typically comes from email marketing, meaning a business with a 10,000-person email list and $1.7M revenue that does no email nurture is leaving an estimated $500K to $1.5M in near-zero-cost revenue uncaptured.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: mature e-commerce business
existing email list of opted-in customers
claims.mechanism: Email reactivates customers who were acquired at cost; subsequent purchases have zero CAC, so email revenue is nearly all margin.

numbers.axis: share of total e-commerce revenue from email marketing by business maturity

anchors.region: Trophy Outlet (Cody Shilson) with 10,000 contacts and no nurture program

bounded_by: Requires an email list of customers who opted in
Does not apply to pure marketplace sellers with no first-party email capture (e.g., TikTok Shop only)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the presence of a 70% revenue concentration in a single customer is an automatic disqualifier for acquisition of a small business, particularly when the incumbent owner is retiring, because the relationship between that customer and the retiring owner is the primary reason the revenue exists.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: small business acquisition
single customer represents 70%+ of revenue
incumbent owner is retiring
claims.mechanism: In small businesses, key customer relationships are often personal to the owner; when the owner retires, those relationships may exit with them, eliminating the acquired revenue.

numbers.axis: single-customer revenue concentration as acquisition risk

anchors.region: 70% revenue from one customer with retiring owner
diversified customer base with no customer >20%

bounded_by: May not apply if the customer relationship is contractually locked in long-term with no personal dependencies

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when a business has an acquisition channel with a strong LTV-to-CAC ratio (such as 13-to-1 on SEO), the correct strategic response is to invest as much as possible into that channel rather than diversifying, because the ratio means each additional dollar in produces thirteen dollars out.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: proven acquisition channel
LTV:CAC ratio materially above 3:1

numbers.axis: LTV-to-CAC ratio as signal for channel investment level

anchors.value: should invest at maximum available budget

bounded_by: Assumes the channel is not capacity-constrained or artificially limited by vendor

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for consumer impulse or gag-gift products, price sensitivity is substantially lower than for repeat B2B commodity products; a gag-gift buyer in the moment of purchase is largely indifferent to whether the item costs $8 or $16, giving gag-gift businesses far more pricing power.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: impulse/gag-gift purchase context
consumer buyer in purchase moment
claims.mechanism: Impulse purchases are driven by emotional state (it is funny now), not value calculation; the emotional driver overwhelms the price comparison that governs commodity purchases.

anchors.value: very price sensitive; buyers shop on price

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that pursuing two distinct business models simultaneously (e.g., B2C viral gag-gift media play and B2B recurring league/organization trophy accounts) will result in serving neither well, and that a business owner must choose one strategic path and cut the other.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: small business without resources to staff two distinct acquisition motions
bounded_by: Does not apply to large organizations with dedicated teams for each model

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for product businesses fulfilling their own orders, inserting a high-value in-box offer (such as buy-one-get-two-free on related products) is a near-zero-cost mechanism to generate repeat purchases from customers who have already demonstrated buying intent.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: physical product business with in-house fulfillment
customer has already purchased and received product
claims.mechanism: Customer is in a receptive state at unboxing; product has already proven its value; a printed offer requires no digital ad spend and reaches a pre-qualified buyer.
bounded_by: Does not apply to FBA-fulfilled Amazon orders where seller has no control over packaging inserts

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that closing down a physical retail location that generates minimal walk-in revenue (approximately $150K/year) and is breaking even or losing money produces an immediate improvement in net profit roughly equal to the annual lease cost saved, because the revenue lost is negligible relative to the cost eliminated.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: physical retail location generating minimal incremental revenue
location is not critical for brand perception or operations
claims.mechanism: Fixed lease costs of approximately $50,000/year drop entirely to bottom line when location closes; the $150K revenue can largely be captured through other channels while the cost disappears.

numbers.axis: profit impact of closing breakeven retail location

anchors.value: +$50K/year to net profit from lease elimination, representing roughly +50% improvement to prior $110K profit

bounded_by: Assumes the closed location's revenue can be partially retained through e-commerce or other channels

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that on social media platforms including TikTok, there is no practical upper limit on posting frequency set by the platform itself; the platform's economic incentive is to distribute content to retain user attention, meaning posting 100 times per day will not be penalized algorithmically.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: short-form video platforms with algorithmic distribution (e.g., TikTok, Instagram Reels)
claims.mechanism: Platforms are incentivized to surface content that retains users; additional posts are shown to different segments of the audience, not the same people repeatedly, so each post expands reach rather than cannibalizing prior posts.

numbers.axis: typical audience reach per post vs. total follower count

anchors.value: typically 1-2% of existing followers see it

bounded_by: Quality must remain consistent; posting 100 times per day of low-quality content still fails
May vary by platform policy changes over time

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for a consumer product with viral and shareability characteristics (funny, giftable, social-moment-driven), organic TikTok content combined with TikTok Shop affiliate influencers is a sufficient mechanism to grow from $1M to $10M in revenue, if focused on exclusively.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: consumer product with high social shareability
TikTok Shop affiliate program available
founder commits exclusively to this channel vs. splitting focus
claims.mechanism: Funny/shareable products generate organic viral views at near-zero cost; TikTok Shop enables affiliate creators to sell with commission, creating a self-funding content flywheel where viral content informs influencer content and vice versa.

numbers.axis: revenue scale achievable via TikTok organic + affiliate channel for Trophy Outlet gag gifts

anchors.region: Trophy Outlet TikTok, December 2024 (one viral video, 16M views)
projected if fully systematized and exclusive focus
anchors.value: $3M/year from TikTok channel alone; $10M potential with mastery

bounded_by: Requires high content production volume (trends + memes)
Platform-dependent; TikTok Shop conditions may change

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that for TikTok content strategy, the hook is the primary determinant of performance; once a winning hook is found, it should be reused and iterated in multiple variations rather than discarded for novelty.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: short-form video platform (TikTok, Instagram Reels)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the correct email cadence for an e-commerce business selling a lower-frequency-purchase product (e.g., trophies) is 1 email per week, focused on entertainment or value content rather than promotional pitches, to maintain open rates without fatiguing the list.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: e-commerce business
product with purchase frequency of less than monthly
existing customer list with no current nurture program
claims.mechanism: Lower-frequency products do not generate enough purchase occasions to sustain daily or tri-weekly promotional emails; entertainment or value content keeps the list warm without implying irrelevant buying pressure.

numbers.axis: email frequency by product purchase recency

bounded_by: Increase frequency if open rates and click-through rates remain healthy

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that image-heavy emails have lower deliverability rates than plain-text emails, and that a better approach is to include a clickable text link to an image, which preserves curiosity-driven clicks while maintaining inbox placement.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: email marketing to customer lists
claims.mechanism: Spam filters and email clients score image-heavy emails as more likely to be promotional, reducing inbox placement; plain-text emails mimic personal correspondence and avoid these filters.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that founders are disproportionately fearful of raising prices relative to the actual business risk, because the worst outcome of a failed price test is simply reverting to the prior price, whereas the cost of never testing is a permanent uncaptured profit opportunity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that price sensitivity varies by customer segment and purchase type, and that the correct optimization target is gross profit times units sold (not units sold alone), meaning a business may maximize profit by selling fewer units at a higher price even if total volume declines.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: business with meaningful gross margin headroom
multiple customer segments with different price sensitivities

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for PPC / branded search terms, a business should always bid on its own brand name and derivatives, even if it already ranks organically for those terms, because not all organic clicks are guaranteed and the cost per conversion on branded keywords is extremely low.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: business with established brand name
search intent-based product (not impulse purchase)
bounded_by: Less applicable for pure impulse-buy products not searched by brand name

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the primary metric e-commerce businesses should use to diagnose pricing power is the relationship between close rate (or conversion rate) and gross profit per unit: when conversion rate is high, it signals that price is below market-clearing, meaning there is room to raise prices before sales volume meaningfully drops.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: e-commerce or transactional business with measurable conversion rate

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the return on focus (concentrating founder attention on the single highest-leverage activity) exceeds the return on any other resource allocation, meaning adding a third business line or maintaining a non-strategic retail location always has a negative expected value when the business has identified a high-return primary path.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder-led business with identified high-return primary channel

examples.text: Cody Shilson's Trophy Outlet (St. Louis, 2024) generated $270,000 in TikTok Shop revenue in its first year on the platform, with $250,000 of that arriving in December alone from a single video that reached 16 million views. The company fulfilled approximately 13,000 orders that month entirely through its in-house production facility. Alex Hormozi cited this as evidence that the viral product category (gag office trophies) had the shareability characteristics needed to build a $10M TikTok-first business if systematized rather than left to chance.

Cody Shilson described a prospective acquisition target in the St. Louis trophy market: a competitor generating approximately $3M in annual revenue whose owner was retiring. The deal-breaker identified by Alex Hormozi was that 70% of the target's revenue flowed from a single customer. Hormozi refused to endorse the acquisition, reasoning that the customer relationship was personal to the retiring owner and would likely exit with him, making the acquired revenue illusory.

Trophy Outlet's SEO channel showed a 13-to-1 LTV-to-CAC ratio and was fully outsourced to an agency, requiring minimal founder time. Alex Hormozi used this as a worked example of the channel investment principle: when a proven channel returns $13 for every $1 invested and is not capacity-constrained, the correct response is to triple or quadruple the investment immediately rather than maintain current spending while opening new, unproven channels.

At the start of Cody Shilson's tenure running Trophy Outlet, he discovered a product where the cost of goods was approximately $50 but it was being sold for $45, generating a guaranteed loss on every unit. He immediately nearly doubled the price. Alex Hormozi cited this as evidence that multi-generational family businesses frequently inherit pricing that was never commercially rational, and that systematic price testing is the single highest-leverage move for such businesses.

Alex Hormozi described a Bollywood Instagram page that posts 100 times per day and generates approximately 9 billion views, as a concrete counterexample to the widespread belief that posting more than a few times per day triggers algorithmic penalties. He argued that this demonstrates the platform distributes each post to different audience segments rather than the same users, so high posting frequency expands reach rather than cannibalizing it.

Trophy Outlet had accumulated approximately 10,000 email contacts from years of direct web sales and internal customer relationships, but had no regular email nurture program at the time of the Hormozi consultation. Hormozi estimated this represented $500K to $1.5M in uncaptured annual revenue based on the standard 30-50% email revenue contribution benchmark for mature e-commerce businesses. He characterized this as the closest thing to finding a bag of money.

practices.text: Run an 80/20 split test on your highest-sales-velocity items by raising the price and measuring conversion rate change; optimize for gross profit times units sold, not units sold alone.

For TikTok content strategy, hire someone younger and culturally in tune with current trends to identify and model trending memes and formats; do not rely on a millennial founder's own awareness of what is currently viral.
Place a printed in-box offer card in every fulfilled shipment showing the top two to three related products and a strong BOGO offer; include a QR code to track conversions.

For new email subscribers, use a double opt-in confirmation flow and as the first email ask the subscriber to reply with their funniest trophy story; use the reply to trigger an automation sending a clickable image link, establishing an interactive pattern before any sales pitch.

Use ICE scoring (Impact, Confidence, Ease) to sequence growth initiatives: start with high-impact, high-confidence, low-effort changes (closing a losing location, raising prices) before committing to high-effort, longer-horizon bets (TikTok mastery).

When considering acquiring a small business, always ask for the full customer revenue concentration breakdown; if any single customer represents more than 30-40% of revenue and the seller is retiring, treat it as a near-automatic disqualifier.
Calculate TikTok Shop LTV by dividing total channel revenue by total unique customers; use this as a baseline average order value even if repeat purchase data is unavailable yet.

For email nurture in a lower-purchase-frequency product category, write all 52 weekly emails in a concentrated 1-2 day session at the start of the year so the program is never bottlenecked by content creation.
